'''''Opuntia ficus-indica''''', the '''Indian fig opuntia''', '''fig opuntia''', or '''prickly pear''', is a species of [[cactus]] that has long been a domesticated crop plant grown in agricultural economies throughout [[Arid climate|arid]] and [[Semi-arid climate|semiarid]] parts of the world.<ref name="cabi">{{cite web|title=''Opuntia ficus-indica'' (prickly pear)|url=https://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/37714|publisher=CABI|access-date=1 December 2018|date=27 September 2018}}</ref> ''O. ficus-indica'' is the most widespread and most commercially important cactus.<ref name=GRIN /><ref name=cabi /> It is grown primarily as a fruit crop, and also for the vegetable [[nopal]]es and other uses. Cacti are good crops for dry areas because they efficiently convert water into [[biomass]]. ''O. ficus-indica'' is the most widespread of the long-domesticated cactuses. ''[[Opuntia]]'' species [[hybrid (biology)|hybridize]] easily, but the wild origin of ''O. ficus-indica'' is likely to have been in central Mexico, where its closest genetic relatives are found.<ref name="Griffith, 2004">{{cite journal|author=Griffith, M. P.|year=2004|title=The Origins of an Important Cactus Crop, ''Opuntia ficus-indica'' (Cactaceae): New Molecular Evidence|journal=American Journal of Botany|volume=91|issue=11|pages=1915–1921|doi=10.3732/ajb.91.11.1915|pmid=21652337|s2cid=10454390}}</ref>

== Names ==
Most culinary references to the "prickly pear" refer to this species. The Spanish name ''tuna'' is also used for the fruit of this cactus and for ''[[Opuntia]]'' in general; according to [[Alexander von Humboldt]], it was a word of [[Taíno language|Taino]] origin taken into the Spanish language around 1500.<ref>''Baron F. H. A. von Humboldt's personal narrative of travels to the equinoctial regions of America'' tr. 1852 by Ross, Thomasina: "The following are Haytian words, in their real form, which have passed into the Castilian language since the end of the 15th century... Tuna". Quoted in OED 2nd ed.</ref>

Common English names for the plant and its fruit are ''Indian fig opuntia'', ''Barbary fig'', ''cactus pear'', ''prickly pear'', and ''spineless cactus'', among many others.<ref name=cabi /> In Mexican Spanish, the plant is called [[nopal]], a name that may be used in [[American English]] as [[culinary]] terms. Peninsular Spanish mostly uses ''higo chumbo'' for the fruit and ''chumbera'' for the plant.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Vázquez Ruiz |first1=José |title=Etimología de chumbera y chumbo |journal=Revista de Filología Española |date=30 December 1957 |volume=41 |issue=1/4 |pages=410–417 |doi=10.3989/rfe.1957.v41.i1/4.1055|doi-access=free }}</ref>

In Greek, the plant is called ''φραγκοσυκιά'' and the fruit ''φραγκόσυκο'', literally "Frankish fig", a label historically applied to foreign produce.<ref>{{cite web |title=φραγκόσυκο |url=https://www.greek-language.gr/greekLang/modern_greek/tools/lexica/triantafyllides/search.html?lq=%CF%86%CF%81%CE%B1%CE%B3%CE%BA%CF%8C%CF%83%CF%85%CE%BA%CE%BF |website=Λεξικό της Κοινής Νεοελληνικής |publisher=Centre for the Greek Language |language=el |access-date=18 September 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=φραγκοσυκιά |url=https://pyli.greeklanguage.gr/index.php?catid=69&id=611&option=com_content&view=article |website=Λεξικό της Κοινής Νεοελληνικής |publisher=Centre for the Greek Language |language=el |access-date=18 September 2025}}</ref> In Cyprus, the fruits are commonly known as ''παπουτσόσυκα'' and the plant as ''παπουτσοσυκιά''; the name is glossed in Cypriot dialect sources and popularly explained as "shoe figs" in reference to the thick, shoe-like pads.<ref>{{cite web |title=Παπουτσόσυκον (το) |url=https://www.polignosi.com/cgibin/hweb?-A=32214&-V=cylang |website=Πολιτιστικό Αρχείο Κυπριακής Διαλέκτου (Polignosi) |language=el |access-date=18 September 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Papoutsosyko – prickly pear |url=https://www.cyprusfoodmuseum.com/en/sylloges/trofima/papoutsosyko-prickly-pear |website=Cyprus Food Museum |access-date=18 September 2025}}</ref>

== Description ==
[[File:Opuntia ficus-indica4.jpg|thumb|Flower|left]]
[[File:Opuntia ficus-indica fruit9.jpg|thumb|Fruit|left]]

''O. ficus-indica'' is [[polyploid]], [[hermaphrodite|hermaphroditic]], and [[autogamous]].<ref name="Miller, L.">{{cite web|author=Miller, =L.|title=''Opuntia ficus-indica''|url=http://ecoport.org/ep?Plant=8094&entityType=PLCR**&entityDisplayCategory=full|website=Ecocrop, FAO|access-date=14 November 2015}}</ref> As ''Opuntia'' species grow in semiarid environments, the main limiting factor in their environment is water. They have developed several adaptations to dry conditions, notably [[succulent|succulence]].<ref name="Cactus Opuntia spp. as Forage">{{cite web|last1=Mondragón-Jacobo and Pérez-González|first1=C. and S.|title=Cactus (Opuntia spp.) as Forage|url=https://www.fao.org/docrep/005/y2808e/y2808e00.htm|website=FAO Plant Production and Protection Paper 169|access-date=14 November 2015}}</ref>

A perennial shrub, ''O. ficus-indica'' can grow up to 5 m in height, with thick, succulent, and oblong to [[spatulate]] stems called [[cladode]]s. It has a water-repellent and sun-reflecting waxy [[epidermis]]. Cladodes 1–2 years old produce flowers, with the fruit's colours ranging from pale green to deep red.<ref name="Miller, L." />

The plants flower in three distinct colours: white, yellow, and red. The flowers first appear in early May through the early summer in the Northern Hemisphere, and the fruits ripen from August through October.{{citation needed|date=December 2015}} The fruits are typically eaten, minus the thick outer skin, after chilling in a refrigerator for a few hours. They have a taste similar to sweet [[watermelon]]. The bright red/purple or white/yellowish flesh contains many tiny hard seeds that are usually swallowed but should be avoided by those who have problems digesting seeds.{{Citation needed|date=April 2025}}

== Uses ==
[[File:Barbary Fig Ruby.jpg|thumb|Fruit as food]]
=== Human consumption ===
{{redirect|Cactus juice|the album|Cactus Juice}}
{{more citations needed|section|date=December 2018}}
[[File:Nopales Cortados.jpg|thumb|Sliced nopales]]
''O. ficus-indica'' is consumed widely as food.<ref name="cabi" /> The fruits are commercialized in many parts of the world, eaten raw, and have one of the highest concentrations of [[vitamin C]] of any fruit.<ref name="cabi" /> The young "leaves" (actually cladodes, which technically are stems) are cooked and eaten as a vegetable known as ''[[Nopalito|nopalitos]]''.<ref name="cabi" /> They are sliced into strips, skinned or unskinned, and fried with eggs and [[jalapeño]]s, served as a breakfast treat. They have a texture and flavor like green beans. The fruits or leaves can be boiled, used raw, or blended with fruit juice, cooked on a frying pan, used as a side dish with chicken, or added to [[taco]]s. Jams and jellies are produced from the fruit, which resemble strawberries and figs in color and flavor.<ref name="cabi" /> Mexicans use ''Opuntia'' fruit to make an alcoholic drink called ''[[colonche]]''.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://ask.extension.org/questions/115766|title=Are prickly pear leaves edible?|date=27 February 2013|access-date=25 April 2019|archive-date=6 August 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200806140458/https://ask.extension.org/questions/115766}}</ref>[[File:Opuntia ficus-indica (Indian Fig) flowering at Secunderabad, AP W IMG 6673.jpg|thumb|Flowering]]In [[Sicily]], a prickly pear-flavored liqueur called ''ficodi'' is produced, flavored somewhat like a medicinal [[aperitif]]. In [[Malta]], a liqueur called ''bajtra'' (the Maltese name for prickly pear) is made from this fruit, which grows wild in almost every field. On the island of [[Saint Helena]], the prickly pear also gives its name to locally distilled liqueur, ''[[Tungi Spirit]]''.

=== Fodder ===
The cattle industry of the Southwest United States has begun to cultivate ''O. ficus-indica'',<ref name=cabi /><ref name="tamu">{{cite web|url=https://texnat.tamu.edu/library/symposia/brush-sculptors-innovations-for-tailoring-brushy-rangelands-to-enhance-wildlife-habitat-and-recreational-value/pricklypear-ecology/|title=Pricklypear ecology|author=Darrell N. Ueckert|publisher=Texas Agricultural Experiment Station, Texas A&M University|access-date=15 February 2020}}</ref> both as a feed source for cattle and a boundary fence. Cattle are normally fed a spineless variety of the cactus.<ref name=tamu /> The cactus pads are low in dry matter and crude protein but useful as a supplement in drought conditions. In addition to the food value, the moisture content adequately eliminates watering the cattle during [[drought]].<ref name=tamu /> Numerous wildlife species use the prickly pear for food.<ref name=tamu />  In severe drought years, the spines of wild prickly pear are sometimes burned off for emergency feed.

=== Soil erosion prevention ===
''O. ficus-indica'' is planted in hedges to provide a cheap but effective [[erosion]] control in the [[Mediterranean basin]]. Under those hedges and adjacent areas, soil physical properties, nitrogen, and organic matter are considerably improved. The structural stability of the soil is enhanced, runoff and erosion are reduced, and water storage capacity and permeability are enhanced.<ref name="Le Houérou" />
Prickly pear plantations also positively impact the plant growth of other species by improving severe environmental conditions, which facilitate the colonization and development of herbaceous species.<ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Neffar S, Chenchouni H, Beddiar A, Redjel N|year=2013|title=Rehabilitation of Degraded Rangeland in Drylands by Prickly Pear (Opuntia ficus-indica L.) Plantations: Effect on Soil and Spontaneous Vegetation|journal=Ecologia Balkanica|volume=5|issue=2}}</ref>

''O. ficus-indica'' is being advantageously used in Tunisia and Algeria to slow and direct sand movement and enhance the restoration of vegetative cover, thus minimizing deterioration of built terraces with its deep and strong rooting system.<ref>Nefzaoui, A., Ben Salem, H., & Inglese, P. (2001). "Opuntia-A strategic fodder and efficient tool to combat desertification in the Wana region." Cactus, 73–89.</ref>

=== Other ===
The plant may be used as an ingredient in [[adobe]] to bind and waterproof roofs.<ref name="Griffith, 2004" /> ''O. ficus-indica'' (as well as other species in ''Opuntia'' and ''Nopalea'') is cultivated in [[wikt:nopalry|nopalries]] to serve as a host plant for [[cochineal]] insects, which produce desirable red and purple dyes,<ref name=cabi /> a practice dating to the [[pre-Columbian era]].<ref>{{cite journal|author=Kiesling, R.|year=1999|title=Origen, Domesticación y Distribución de ''Opuntia ficus-indica'' (Cactaceae)|journal=Journal of the Professional Association for Cactus Development|volume=3|pages=50–60}}</ref>

[[Mucilage]] from prickly pear may work as a natural, non-toxic dispersant for oil spills.<ref>{{cite web|last=University of South Florida|title=Cactus a Natural Oil Dispersant|url=http://news.usf.edu/article/templates/?a=4387&z=123|publisher=USF News|access-date=25 April 2019}}</ref>

Mexico has a semicommercial pilot plant for [[biofuel]] production from ''Opuntia'' biomass, in operation since 2016.<ref>{{cite web|title=This Mexican company is making biofuel from cactus plants|date=25 March 2019|url=https://europeansting.com/2019/03/25/this-mexican-company-is-making-biofuel-from-cactus-plants/|publisher=The European Sting|access-date=25 April 2019}}</ref>

== Cultivation ==
[[File:Opuntia ficus-indica (Indian Fig) at Secunderabad, AP W IMG 6674.jpg|thumb|In [[Secunderabad]], India]]

=== Distribution ===
Commercial use for ''O. ficus-indica'' is for the large, sweet fruits called tunas.  An area with a significant tuna-growing cultivation is Mexico.<ref>{{cite encyclopedia|title=Beles|encyclopedia=Encyclopaedia Aethiopica: A-C|location=Wiesbaden|publisher=Harrassowitz Verlag|year=2003}}</ref> The cactus grows wild and cultivated to heights of {{convert|12|–|16|ft}}. In [[Namibia]], ''O. ficus-indica'' is a common drought-resistant fodder plant.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.namibian.com.na/indexx.php?id=9793&page_type=story_detail&category_id=1|title=Staying afloat during a drought|author=Rothauge, Axel|date=25 February 2014|work=[[The Namibian]]|access-date=25 February 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140302053258/http://www.namibian.com.na/indexx.php?id=9793&page_type=story_detail&category_id=1|archive-date=2 March 2014}}</ref> ''O. ficus-indica'' grows in many [[Frost#Frost-free areas|frost-free]] areas of the world, including the [[Southern United States]].<ref>{{cite book |title=The Gardeners Dictionary |chapter=Opuntia ficus-indica, tree prickly pear cactus, fruit |via=Opuntia Web |chapter-url=https://www.opuntiads.com/opuntia-ficus-indica/ |edition=8th |year=1768 }}</ref> 

Prickly pears are a massive weed problem for some parts of Australia, especially [[southeast Queensland]], some inland parts of [[New South Wales]], [[Victoria State|Victoria]], and south-eastern and eastern [[South Australia]].<ref name="Qld-gov-Weeds-of-Aus">{{ cite web | url=https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/weeds/data/media/Html/opuntia_ficusindica.htm | title=Opuntia ficus-indica }}</ref><ref name="NSW-WeedWise">{{cite web | url=http://weeds.dpi.nsw.gov.au/Weeds/Details/274 | title=NSW WeedWise | access-date=2020-10-08 | archive-date=2020-09-23 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200923072742/https://weeds.dpi.nsw.gov.au/Weeds/Details/274 }}</ref><ref name="Atlas-Living-Australia">{{ cite web | url=https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Opuntia%20ficus-indica | title=Atlas of Living Australia }}</ref><ref name="Brisbane-weeds">{{ cite web | url=https://weeds.brisbane.qld.gov.au/weeds/prickly-pear | title=prickly pear – Weed Identification – Brisbane City Council }}</ref>
[[File:OpunitaFicusIndicaKythira.jpg|thumb|''O. ficus-indica'' in [[Kythira|Kythera]], Greece]]
The plant is considered an [[invasive species]] in northern Africa.<ref name="cabi" /><ref>{{Cite journal |first1=Ana |last1=Novoa |first2=Johannes J. |last2=Le Roux |first3=Mark P. |last3=Robertson |first4=John R.U. |last4=Wilson |first5=David M. |last5=Richardson |date=2015-02-05 |title=Introduced and invasive cactus species: a global review |journal=AoB Plants |volume=7 |doi=10.1093/aobpla/plu078 |pmc=4318432 |pmid=25471679}}</ref>

=== Growth ===
Factors that limit the growth of prickly pear are rainfall, soil, atmospheric humidity, and temperature.<ref name ="Monjauze">Monjauze, A. & Le Houérou, H. N. (1965). "Le rôle des Opuntia dans l'économie agricole nord africaine." Bulletin de l'Ecole Nationale Supérieure d'Agronomie de Tunis, 8–9: 85–164.</ref> Its minimum rainfall requirement is 200 mm per year as long as the soils are sandy and deep. The ideal growth conditions regarding rainfall are {{convert|200|–|400|mm|abbr=on}} per year.<ref name="Le Houérou">{{cite journal|author=Le Houérou H. N.|year=1996|title=The role of cacti (Opuntiaspp.) in erosion control, land reclamation, rehabilitation and agricultural development in the Mediterranean Basin|journal=Journal of Arid Environments|volume=33|issue=2|pages=135–159|doi=10.1006/jare.1996.0053|bibcode=1996JArEn..33..135L}}</ref>

''O. ficus-indica'' is sensitive to lack of oxygen in the root zone, requiring well-drained soils.<ref name="Le Houérou" /> It is similar to [[crassulacean acid metabolism]] species, which are not salt-tolerant in their root zone, and growth may cease under high salt concentration.<ref name="Le Houérou" /> ''O. ficus-indica'' usually grows in regions where [[relative humidity]] is above 60%, and saturation deficit{{explain|date=July 2016}} occurs.<ref name="Le Houérou" /> It is absent in regions where less than 40% humidity occurs for more than a month.<ref name="Monjauze" /> Mean daily temperature required to develop is at least 1.5–2.0 °C. At −10 to −12 °C, prickly pear growth is inhibited even if it is exposed to these temperatures only for a few minutes. The maximum temperature limit of prickly pear is above 50 °C.<ref name="Le Houérou" />

=== Harvest and preparation ===
As the fruits of ''O. ficus-indica'' are delicate, they need to be carefully harvested by hand. The small spines on the fruits are removed by rubbing them on an abrasive surface or sweeping them through the grass. Before consumption, they are peeled.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Russel, Felkner|author2=C.E., P.|title=The Prickly-pears (''Opuntia'' spp., Cactaceae): A Source of Human and Animal Food in Semiarid Regions|date=1987|volume=41|issue=3|pages=443–445|doi=10.1007/bf02859062|journal=Economic Botany|s2cid=37653492}}</ref>

The pads of the plant (mainly used as fodder) also must be harvested by hand. The pads are cut with a knife, detaching the pad from the plant in the joint. If ''O. ficus-indica'' is cultivated for [[forage]] production, spineless cultivars are preferred, but wild plants are also used as fodder. In these cases, the spines must be removed from the pads to avoid animal damage. Primarily, this is achieved by burning the spines off the pads.<ref name="Cactus Opuntia spp. as Forage" />

== Biogeography ==
[[DNA]] analysis indicated ''O. ficus-indica'' was domesticated from ''Opuntia'' species native to central Mexico.<ref name="Griffith, 2004" /> The [[Codex Mendoza]], and other early sources, show ''Opuntia'' [[wikt:cladode|cladodes]], as well as [[cochineal]] dye (which must be cultivated on ''Opuntia''), in [[Aztec]] tribute rolls.{{citation needed|date=December 2015}}  The plant spread to many parts of the Americas in pre-Columbian times. Since Columbus, it has spread to many parts of the world, especially the Mediterranean, where it has become naturalized.

== Cultural significance ==
[[File:Coat of arms of Mexico.svg|thumb|The [[coat of arms of Mexico]]|180x180px]]
{{Main article|Opuntia#Culture|Sabra (person)}}
The prickly pear appears in the [[coat of arms of Mexico]] which appears on the [[flag of Mexico]]. It is also the official plant of [[Texas]] by legislation from 1995.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Texas State Symbols |url=https://www.tsl.texas.gov/ref/abouttx/symbols}}</ref> The plant is both an Israeli and Palestinian symbol. In Israel, the term [[Sabra (person)|sabra]] is a name for the plant and for Jews born in Israel.<ref>{{cite book |first=Katherine |last=Natanel |title=Sustaining Conflict: Apathy and Domination in Israel-Palestine |page=165 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RbQwDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA165 |year=2016 |publisher=[[University of California Press]] |isbn=978-0-520-28526-2 |access-date=18 March 2025}}</ref>
